intro: Vectors are quantities with both a size and a direction, like a push, a velocity, or a step on a map. This branch builds the basic toolkit for working with them, the foundation for everything else in this era.

VII.1.01.what: A vector is an arrow with a length and a direction, or equally a short list of numbers. A wind of 10 mph blowing northeast is a vector.

levels.a: Draws and reads vectors as arrows with a length and a direction.
levels.b: Writes a vector as a list of numbers, such as 3 steps right and 2 up.
levels.c: Tells apart an arrow pinned to a spot from one that can slide anywhere.
levels.d: Works with vectors that have any number of entries, not just two or three.

VII.1.02.what: Adding vectors means combining two moves into one, like walking 3 blocks east and then 4 blocks north.

levels.a: Adds two arrows by placing the tail of the second at the tip of the first.
levels.b: Adds two arrows from the same starting point by completing a parallelogram.
levels.c: Adds vectors as lists by adding matching entries.
levels.d: Subtracts vectors and sees the result as the arrow from one tip to the other.

VII.1.03.what: Multiplying a vector by an ordinary number (a scalar) stretches or shrinks it, like doubling a speed while keeping the direction.

levels.a: Stretches or shrinks an arrow by multiplying it by a number.
levels.b: Sees that multiplying by a negative number flips the arrow around.
levels.c: Multiplies each entry of a vector list by the number.
levels.d: Recognizes when two vectors point along the same line (are parallel).

VII.1.04.what: The magnitude of a vector is its length, found with the Pythagorean theorem. It tells how big the push or movement is.

levels.a: Finds the length of a flat, two-entry vector.
levels.b: Finds lengths of vectors in 3D and with more entries.
levels.c: Finds the distance between two points as the length of the arrow joining them.
levels.d: Uses basic facts about length, such as a detour never being shorter.

VII.1.05.what: A unit vector has length exactly 1 and just records a direction, like a compass heading with no distance attached.

levels.a: Shrinks or stretches a vector to length 1 while keeping its direction.
levels.b: Uses the three standard unit arrows that point along the x, y and z axes.
levels.c: Builds a direction vector from a given angle.
levels.d: Writes any vector as its length times its direction.

VII.1.06.what: A linear combination mixes vectors using chosen amounts of each, like a recipe: 2 parts of one move plus 3 parts of another.

levels.a: Combines vectors using given amounts (weights) of each.
levels.b: Finds the amounts needed to reach a given target vector.
levels.c: Sets up that search as a set of equations to solve together.
levels.d: Pictures combinations as a slanted grid covering the plane.

VII.1.07.what: The span of some vectors is every point you can reach by combining them. One arrow gives a line; two different arrows usually give a flat plane.

levels.a: Sees that one vector's span is a line through the starting point.
levels.b: Decides whether two flat vectors reach the whole plane or just a line.
levels.c: Describes what two vectors in 3D reach: a plane or a line.
levels.d: Checks whether a given vector can be reached from a set of vectors.

VII.1.08.what: The dot product multiplies two vectors to get a single number that measures how much they point the same way.

levels.a: Computes a dot product by multiplying matching entries and adding them up.
levels.b: Uses its basic rules, such as order not mattering.
levels.c: Finds a vector's length from its dot product with itself.
levels.d: Computes work done as force times distance moved, using the dot product.

VII.1.09.what: The dot product can reveal the angle between two arrows. When it is zero, the arrows are at right angles.

levels.a: Learns the formula linking the dot product to the angle's cosine.
levels.b: Computes the angle between two given vectors.
levels.c: Recognizes perpendicular vectors because their dot product is zero.
levels.d: Uses the fact that a dot product can never exceed the product of the lengths.

VII.1.10.what: Projecting one vector onto another finds its shadow along that direction, like the part of a slanted push that moves a cart forward.

levels.a: Finds how long the shadow of one vector on another is.
levels.b: Finds the shadow itself as a vector.
levels.c: Finds the leftover part of the vector that sits at right angles.
levels.d: Finds the point on a line closest to a given point.

VII.1.11.what: The cross product takes two 3D arrows and gives a third arrow at right angles to both. Its length equals the area they outline.

levels.a: Computes a cross product with a set recipe of multiplications.
levels.b: Uses the right-hand rule to tell which way the result points.
levels.c: Finds the area of a parallelogram from its two side vectors.
levels.d: Finds the volume of a slanted box from its three edge vectors.

VII.1.12.what: Vectors describe straight lines and flat planes in 3D space, the way a pilot might describe a flight path or a runway surface.

levels.a: Writes a line as a starting point plus any amount of a direction vector.
levels.b: Writes a plane's equation from an arrow sticking straight out of it.
levels.c: Finds where lines and planes meet each other.
levels.d: Finds shortest distances between points, lines and planes.
